slides.say: The operation diamond is defined for every positive number x. It is known that for every positive x, diamond of diamond of x is equal to x. Which of the following can be the definition of the operation diamond?

There's no rule here, only a property. Doing the diamond twice brings us back to x. [short pause] We'll solve it two ways, testing each rule with a number, and then by understanding which rules undo themselves.

[short pause] For each choice, let's apply the rule twice and see if we get back to where we started. Let's take x is two. Why two? It's easy to calculate, and it isn't one, because one can stay one under some rules and fool us.

Choice number one, six x. Two goes to twelve, and twelve goes to seventy-two. Seventy-two is not two, so choice number one is out. Choice number two, x plus six. Two goes to eight, and eight goes to fourteen. Not two, out.
at: so choice number one is out
Choice number two, x plus six

slides.say: Choice number three, x over six. Two goes to two sixths, which is one third. And one third over six is one eighteenth. Not two, out. Choice number four, six over x. Two goes to six over two, which is three. And three goes to six over three, which is two. We're back at two.
at: Choice number four, six over x

slides.say: One example can't prove always, but the other three are out, so choice number four is our answer.
at: so choice number four is our answer

slides.say: [pause] Another way is to know which kind of rule undoes itself. Six over x turns a number into six divided by it. Do it again, and we divide six by six over x. Dividing by a fraction is multiplying by its reciprocal. So six times x over six, which is x. It always comes back.
The same happens with any number minus x. Ten minus x, and then ten minus that, is ten minus ten plus x, which is x again.

But six x, x plus six and x over six all keep moving the same way. Times six makes a number bigger, and doing it again makes it even bigger. So they never come back. Choice number four. [pause] Okay. I'll see you in the next question.
